description: Defines common operational anti-patterns, their warning signs, root causes, business impact, and recommended corrective actions.

antiPatterns.name: Hero Organization
antiPatterns.looksLike: A small number of people are personally responsible for keeping critical things running. When they're out, things slow down or stop.
antiPatterns.whyItHappens: Early growth rewards the person who steps up and just makes it work. That behavior gets praised, repeated, and never replaced with a system.
antiPatterns.whyItFeelsReasonable: Heroics feel like commitment and capability. Leaders see the problem get solved and reward the person, not the absence of a system.
antiPatterns.whatItBreaks: The organization's capacity is capped by a handful of people's availability, and their departure becomes a genuine operational risk rather than a staffing inconvenience.
signals: "Ask Sarah, she knows how that works" is a common sentence.
Vacation requests from key people trigger visible anxiety.
Onboarding a replacement takes months because nothing is written down.

antiPatterns.name: Meeting Operating System
antiPatterns.looksLike: The calendar is full of recurring meetings that stand in for an actual management system — status updates, syncs, and check-ins with no clear decision output.
antiPatterns.whyItHappens: When there's no real operating rhythm, adding a meeting feels like the fastest way to create visibility and coordination.
antiPatterns.whyItFeelsReasonable: Meetings feel like alignment and communication is happening. Attendance is easy to measure; decision quality is not.
antiPatterns.whatItBreaks: Time is consumed without decisions being made or tracked, and people mistake attendance for governance.
signals: Nobody can say what decision came out of last week's recurring meeting.
The same status gets reported in three different meetings.
Meetings get added to solve problems; they're rarely removed.

antiPatterns.name: SOP Graveyard
antiPatterns.looksLike: A large library of documented procedures that few people read, fewer follow, and nobody keeps current.
antiPatterns.whyItHappens: Documentation gets created in response to an audit, incident, or onboarding push, then never gets a governance mechanism to keep it accurate.
antiPatterns.whyItFeelsReasonable: Having documentation feels like the job is done. It's an artifact leadership can point to as evidence of maturity.
antiPatterns.whatItBreaks: The organization believes it has standardized processes when it actually has stale documents and undocumented real behavior running in parallel.
signals: SOPs contradict how the work is actually performed.
Nobody has updated key procedures in over a year.
New hires are told to "ignore that doc, just ask around."

antiPatterns.name: Dashboard Theater
antiPatterns.looksLike: Dashboards, reports, and visualizations everywhere — but decisions are still made on gut feel or the loudest voice in the room.
antiPatterns.whyItHappens: Investing in visualization is visible and fundable. Connecting metrics to actual decision-making processes is harder and less visible work.
antiPatterns.whyItFeelsReasonable: Dashboards look like data-driven management. Building them satisfies a desire to feel in control of the numbers.
antiPatterns.whatItBreaks: Metrics without decisions are reporting, not management. The organization pays the cost of measurement without capturing the benefit.
signals: The same dashboard is reviewed weekly with no resulting action.
Different teams maintain competing versions of the same metric.
A metric trending badly for months hasn't triggered any intervention.

antiPatterns.name: Escalation Culture
antiPatterns.looksLike: Problems routinely jump straight to senior leaders because nobody below them feels confident resolving anything independently.
antiPatterns.whyItHappens: Decision rights were never made explicit, so the safest move for anyone uncertain is to push the decision upward.
antiPatterns.whyItFeelsReasonable: Escalation feels like diligence and appropriate caution. Leaders often feel needed and important resolving it personally.
antiPatterns.whatItBreaks: If everything requires escalation, you don't have decision rights. Leadership becomes a bottleneck, and the organization can't move faster than its most senior people's calendars.
signals: Senior leaders are looped into decisions well below their level.
Teams wait for permission rather than acting within a defined scope.
The same category of issue escalates repeatedly instead of getting a standing resolution.

antiPatterns.name: Training Fix
antiPatterns.looksLike: Performance problems are addressed by sending people to training, regardless of whether a skills gap is actually the cause.
antiPatterns.whyItHappens: Training is fast to approve, doesn't require confronting process or management issues, and puts the responsibility for improvement on individuals.
antiPatterns.whyItFeelsReasonable: It feels proactive and developmental. Nobody has to admit the process, tooling, or management system might be the actual problem.
antiPatterns.whatItBreaks: The underlying system condition remains untouched, so the same performance issue resurfaces with the next person or the next quarter.
signals: Training is proposed before anyone investigates root cause.
The same training gets repeated for successive cohorts with no lasting effect.
Skilled, well-trained people still can't execute consistently.

antiPatterns.name: Tooling Fix
antiPatterns.looksLike: A new software tool is purchased to solve a problem that is actually about process, ownership, or governance.
antiPatterns.whyItHappens: Buying a tool feels like tangible progress and can be championed and budgeted quickly, unlike the harder work of redesigning a process.
antiPatterns.whyItFeelsReasonable: Vendors sell outcomes, not just software, and it's easier to believe a tool will fix a human/process problem than to redesign the system.
antiPatterns.whatItBreaks: Automating a bad process just makes the bad process faster. The tool adds cost and complexity without resolving the actual constraint.
signals: A new tool is rolled out without changing the process it's meant to support.
Adoption is low because the tool doesn't match how work actually happens.
The same category of problem persists across multiple prior tool replacements.

antiPatterns.name: Everything Is Priority
antiPatterns.looksLike: Every initiative is labeled top priority, so teams have no real basis for sequencing or saying no.
antiPatterns.whyItHappens: Leaders avoid the harder conversation of making tradeoffs explicit, so they resolve conflicting demands by declaring all of them urgent.
antiPatterns.whyItFeelsReasonable: Calling something a priority feels like leadership and urgency. It avoids the discomfort of telling a stakeholder their request is not the priority.
antiPatterns.whatItBreaks: Capacity gets fragmented across too many initiatives, nothing finishes on schedule, and teams burn out trying to serve every simultaneous demand.
signals: More than a handful of concurrent initiatives are all labeled "P1."
Teams can't articulate what they'd stop doing to take on new work.
Prioritization conversations end without any actual deprioritization.

antiPatterns.name: Shadow Process
antiPatterns.looksLike: The documented, official process and the process people actually follow have quietly diverged.
antiPatterns.whyItHappens: The official process didn't account for a real exception or constraint, so people built a workaround and never fed it back into the design.
antiPatterns.whyItFeelsReasonable: The workaround solves an immediate problem, and updating official documentation feels like unnecessary overhead compared to just getting the work done.
antiPatterns.whatItBreaks: Nobody has an accurate picture of how work actually happens, which makes it impossible to reliably improve, audit, or scale the process.
signals: Spreadsheets or side channels exist to compensate for a gap in the "real" process.
Auditors or new hires are surprised by how work actually gets done.
Two teams performing the "same" process do it in incompatible ways.

antiPatterns.name: Leader Bottleneck
antiPatterns.looksLike: Progress across multiple teams depends on the availability and personal attention of a single leader.
antiPatterns.whyItHappens: The leader has historically been the fastest, most trusted decision-maker, so decision rights informally concentrated around them instead of being distributed.
antiPatterns.whyItFeelsReasonable: It feels efficient in the moment — the leader genuinely does make good, fast decisions. The cost only shows up as the organization grows past what one person can attend to.
antiPatterns.whatItBreaks: Scale exposes ambiguity: what worked when the leader could personally touch every decision breaks down as volume and team count grow, and the leader becomes the constraint on organizational throughput.
signals: Multiple teams are blocked waiting on the same person's sign-off.
That leader's calendar is the actual bottleneck on delivery timelines.
Decisions reverse or stall whenever that leader is unavailable.

antiPatterns.name: KPI Explosion
antiPatterns.looksLike: Dozens of metrics are tracked across teams with no clear hierarchy, ownership, or connection to decisions.
antiPatterns.whyItHappens: Every team adds metrics that matter to them locally, and nobody is responsible for pruning or organizing the resulting sprawl.
antiPatterns.whyItFeelsReasonable: More measurement feels like more rigor. It's easier to add a metric than to argue one should be removed.
antiPatterns.whatItBreaks: Attention gets diluted across too many numbers, genuinely important signals get lost in the noise, and reporting overhead grows without improving decisions.
signals: No one can name the organization's five most important metrics without checking a document.
Metrics get added regularly; almost none are ever retired.
Different reports show conflicting numbers for what should be the same metric.

antiPatterns.name: RACI Illusion
antiPatterns.looksLike: A completed RACI chart exists for key processes, but people still don't behave as though decision authority is actually clear.
antiPatterns.whyItHappens: Building the RACI was treated as the deliverable itself, rather than the starting point for reinforcing and governing the behavior it describes.
antiPatterns.whyItFeelsReasonable: Having a RACI chart is tangible proof of clarity. It's easy to mistake the document for the outcome it's supposed to produce.
antiPatterns.whatItBreaks: Having a RACI does not mean decision authority is clear. Decisions keep escalating or stalling exactly as before, and now there's a document that says they shouldn't.
signals: People can't recall what the RACI says about a decision they're actively stuck on.
The RACI was built once during a project and never revisited.
Behavior during real decisions doesn't match the documented chart.

antiPatterns.name: Automation Trap
antiPatterns.looksLike: A poorly performing or inconsistent process gets automated in an effort to improve it.
antiPatterns.whyItHappens: Automation is seen as inherently an improvement, so it gets applied to whatever process is causing the most visible pain, without first fixing the process design.
antiPatterns.whyItFeelsReasonable: Automation projects are exciting, fundable, and modern. It feels like progress compared to the slower work of redesigning a process.
antiPatterns.whatItBreaks: Automating a bad process just makes the bad process faster. Inconsistency and errors that used to be caught by a human now happen at machine speed and scale.
signals: Automation was scoped before the underlying process was standardized.
The automated process still produces the same category of errors, just faster.
Nobody can explain the rules the automation is actually enforcing.

antiPatterns.name: Local Optimum
antiPatterns.looksLike: A team or function optimizes its own metrics or workflow in a way that creates friction or cost somewhere else in the organization.
antiPatterns.whyItHappens: Teams are measured and rewarded on locally visible outcomes, with no mechanism connecting their optimization to the end-to-end value stream.
antiPatterns.whyItFeelsReasonable: The team is genuinely improving the number they're accountable for, and that number looks like real progress from inside the function.
antiPatterns.whatItBreaks: Organizations are structured vertically, but value usually moves horizontally — a local win can quietly create a larger loss somewhere downstream.
signals: One team's efficiency gain creates rework or delay for another team.
Cross-functional handoffs are the site of recurring friction that no single team owns.
Metrics are set and reviewed entirely within functional silos.
